questions.question: What is application.properties in Spring Boot?
questions.title: application.properties — Spring Boot configuration file
questions.direct_answer: `application.properties` is a standard Spring Boot configuration file. It stores settings as `key=value` pairs, and Spring Boot adds those values to its `Environment` so auto-configuration and application code can use them.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `application.properties` stores configuration as `key=value` pairs.
A common project location is `src/main/resources/application.properties`; it becomes a classpath-root file in the packaged application.
It can contain Spring Boot settings such as `server.port` and custom settings such as `app.mail.timeout`.
Spring Boot places the values in its `Environment`; a higher-priority source can override them.
Do not commit real passwords, tokens, or production secrets to this file.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`application.properties` is one of Spring Boot's standard configuration files. It uses simple `key=value` lines, so settings stay outside the Java classes that use them. A common project location is `src/main/resources/application.properties`; it becomes a classpath-root file in the packaged application.

For example, `server.port=8081` changes the HTTP port and `app.mail.timeout=2s` defines an application-specific timeout. Spring Boot reads the file as config data and adds the values to its `Environment`. Auto-configuration reads many built-in keys, while our own beans can read custom keys with `@Value` or `@ConfigurationProperties`.

The file is a default, not the only source of configuration. A profile-specific file, environment variable, Java system property, or command-line argument may replace the same key according to Spring Boot's property-source order. This lets the application keep safe defaults in the package and supply environment-specific values during deployment.

I would keep related keys under a clear prefix, use real types such as `Duration` when binding them, and avoid storing secrets in source control. The important idea is that `application.properties` separates changeable settings from code while still making them available through one Spring configuration environment.

sections.title: How the file becomes application configuration
sections.content:
Spring Boot treats `application.properties` as config data. During startup it searches its standard locations, loads the file, and makes each property available through the Spring `Environment`. The conventional classpath location is the root of `src/main/resources`, although external configuration directories are also supported.

A property key normally describes one setting. Spring Boot owns keys such as `server.port` and `spring.application.name`. Applications should give custom settings a clear namespace, for example `app.mail.retry-count`, so they do not collide with framework keys.

Values are text in the file, but they do not have to remain Java strings. Spring's conversion and binding support can turn `2s` into a `Duration`, `3` into an integer, or a group of `app.mail.*` keys into one configuration object. This keeps parsing rules out of business code.

The final value may come from somewhere else. If `server.port` is present in the packaged file and also supplied as a command-line option, Spring Boot uses the higher-priority command-line value. The application reads the effective value from the `Environment`; it does not need separate code for every source.

Source-controlled files should contain safe defaults, not credentials. A production secret should come from an appropriate deployment secret mechanism and be exposed to the process through a supported external source. This keeps one application artifact reusable across environments without publishing sensitive data.

sections.title: Configuration values meet in the Spring Environment
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[application.properties] --> E[Spring Environment]
  B[Profile-specific file] --> E
  C[Environment and system properties] --> E
  D[Command-line arguments] --> E
  E --> F[Boot auto-configuration]
  E --> G[Application beans]
```

sections.title: A small application.properties file
sections.content:
```properties
# src/main/resources/application.properties
spring.application.name=order-service
server.port=8081
app.mail.retry-count=3
app.mail.timeout=2s
```

The first two keys configure Spring Boot. The `app.mail.*` keys belong to the application and can be bound to a typed configuration object.

questions.question: How do you create profile-specific configuration in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Profile-specific application properties
questions.direct_answer: Put shared settings in `application.properties`, put environment-specific overrides in a file named `application-{profile}.properties`, and activate that profile externally—for example with `--spring.profiles.active=dev`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Name the file `application-{profile}.properties`, such as `application-dev.properties`.
Keep shared defaults in `application.properties`; the active profile file overrides matching keys.
Activate a profile with a command-line argument, environment setting, system property, or another allowed source.
More than one profile can be active; later profile-specific files can override earlier ones.
Do not place `spring.profiles.active` inside a profile-specific document or one activated by `spring.config.activate.on-profile`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Spring profiles let one application use different configuration for environments or named modes. I keep common values in `application.properties`, then create files such as `application-dev.properties` and `application-prod.properties` for values that really differ.

If the `dev` profile is active, Spring Boot loads the base file and then the `dev` file. A matching key in `application-dev.properties` replaces the base value, while base values that are not repeated remain available. For example, the base file may set an application name and timeout, while the development file changes only logging and the server port.

I normally choose the active profile outside the packaged application, for example `java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev` or the equivalent deployment environment setting. That keeps the same JAR usable in development, testing, and production. Multiple profiles are allowed, so their order matters when they define the same key.

A profile is useful for a coherent group of settings, but it is not a secret store. Passwords and tokens should still come from a secure external source. Also, `spring.profiles.active` cannot be declared inside a profile-specific file or a document already controlled by `spring.config.activate.on-profile`.

sections.title: How a profile changes only the settings it owns
sections.content:
A profile-specific filename follows the pattern `application-{profile}.properties`. The text between the hyphen and extension is the profile name. For a `dev` profile, Spring Boot looks for `application-dev.properties` alongside the ordinary application configuration in each config-data location.

The base and profile files work together. Suppose the base file defines `spring.application.name`, `server.port`, and `app.client.timeout`. If the development file contains only a different port, the application still receives the base name and timeout, but it receives the development port. This is an override, not a completely separate configuration.

The active profile is itself a property, so its source follows Spring Boot's precedence rules. A command-line value can override one placed in a lower-priority base file. `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` is also a common deployment form. Keeping this choice outside the artifact prevents rebuilding the JAR for every environment.

When several profiles are active, profile-specific files are considered in the configured order and a later value can win for the same key. That can be useful for combinations such as `prod,metrics`, but too many overlapping profiles become difficult to reason about. Each profile should have a clear purpose.

Profile names should not be used as access control, and profile files should not contain committed production credentials. They only select configuration. Secret values still require controlled storage, limited access, and safe injection into the running process.

sections.title: Base configuration and one active profile
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  S[Start application] --> B[Load application.properties]
  B --> P{Active profile?}
  P -->|dev| D[Overlay application-dev.properties]
  P -->|prod| R[Overlay application-prod.properties]
  P -->|none| E[Use base values]
  D --> E[Build Spring Environment]
  R --> E
```

sections.title: Base defaults with development and production overrides
sections.content:
```properties
# application.properties
spring.application.name=order-service
server.port=8080
app.client.timeout=2s
```

```properties
# application-dev.properties
server.port=8081
logging.level.com.example.orders=DEBUG
```

```properties
# application-prod.properties
server.port=9000
logging.level.com.example.orders=INFO
```

```bash
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev
```

With `dev` active, the effective port is `8081`; the application name and timeout still come from the base file.

questions.question: How do you read custom properties from application.properties in your code?
questions.title: @Value and @ConfigurationProperties for custom properties
questions.direct_answer: `@Value` reads one custom property, while `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a related group to a typed object. Register a configuration-properties type through scanning, `@EnableConfigurationProperties`, or as a Spring bean.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use `@Value("${app.banner:Orders}")` for a small, independent value with an optional default.
Use `@ConfigurationProperties("payment")` to bind related `payment.*` keys to one typed object.
Register configuration-properties types with scanning, `@EnableConfigurationProperties`, or as Spring beans.
Binding converts values such as `2s` to `Duration`; `@Validated` can reject invalid configuration at startup.
`@ConfigurationProperties` supports relaxed binding and metadata; `@Value` supports SpEL but has only limited relaxed binding.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Spring exposes loaded configuration through its `Environment`, and the two common annotation-based choices are `@Value` and `@ConfigurationProperties`. I use `@Value` when a bean needs one small, independent value. For example, `@Value("${app.banner:Orders}")` injects `app.banner` and uses `Orders` when the key is missing.

For a related group, I prefer `@ConfigurationProperties`. A record annotated with `@ConfigurationProperties("payment")` can bind `payment.base-url`, `payment.timeout`, and `payment.max-retries` to named Java components. Spring converts values to types such as `Duration` and `int`, so the rest of the application receives a clear configuration object instead of several unrelated strings.

The configuration-properties type must be registered. I can use `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan`, list it in `@EnableConfigurationProperties`, or make it a Spring bean. Adding `@Validated` and Jakarta Validation constraints lets startup fail with a useful binding error when a required URL is blank or a retry count is negative.

`@ConfigurationProperties` also supports relaxed binding and generated IDE metadata, which makes it a good fit for reusable groups. `@Value` supports Spring Expression Language and is convenient for isolated values, but it does not provide the same grouped metadata. My choice is based on the shape of the configuration: one value uses `@Value`; a meaningful group gets a typed configuration object.

sections.title: From property keys to safe Java values
sections.content:
`@Value` resolves a placeholder for the bean being created. The form `${app.banner}` requires the property; `${app.banner:Orders}` supplies a fallback. Spring can convert the result to the target field or constructor-parameter type, so it is not limited to strings. Canonical kebab-case property names give the most predictable lookup behavior.

`@ConfigurationProperties` starts with a prefix and binds the matching subtree. With the prefix `payment`, the key `payment.max-retries` maps naturally to the Java component `maxRetries`. This relaxed binding also understands common environment-variable forms such as `PAYMENT_MAX_RETRIES`.

A constructor-bound record is a compact immutable choice for required settings. Registration is still necessary because the annotation describes binding but does not, by itself, make every type a bean. `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` is convenient for an application package; `@EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class)` is explicit and useful in a small configuration.

Validation protects the application before it serves traffic. `@Validated` enables Jakarta Validation checks on the bound object. A blank base URL or negative retry count then produces a startup failure rather than a later business error. Defaults can be supplied in configuration or in a deliberate binding design, but a default should not hide a genuinely required setting.

Configuration metadata is another practical difference. Adding Spring Boot's configuration processor lets an IDE suggest custom keys, types, and descriptions for `@ConfigurationProperties`. `@Value` can evaluate SpEL expressions, but expression-heavy configuration is harder to discover and test. For ordinary application settings, typed binding is usually clearer.

sections.title: @Value and @ConfigurationProperties serve different shapes
sections.content:
| Concern | `@Value` | `@ConfigurationProperties` |
|---|---|---|
| Best fit | One or two independent values | A related group of settings |
| Type conversion | Yes, through Spring conversion | Yes, including nested and collection values |
| Relaxed binding | Limited; use canonical kebab-case | Yes |
| Group validation | Not provided by the placeholder itself | Supports `@Validated` on the bound type |
| IDE metadata | No custom configuration metadata | Generated by the configuration processor |
| SpEL | Supported | Not supported |

questions.question: What is the difference between application.properties and application.yml?
questions.title: application.properties vs application.yml
questions.direct_answer: The difference is syntax: `application.properties` uses flat `key=value` lines, while `application.yml` uses indentation for nested maps and lists. Both configure the same Spring Boot `Environment`; if both formats exist in one location, `.properties` takes precedence.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Both formats feed values into the same Spring `Environment`; neither changes application behavior by itself.
`.properties` uses flat `key=value` entries and repeats the full path on each line.
YAML uses indentation for nesting and is often easier to scan for lists or large configuration trees.
YAML indentation and implicit value parsing require care; properties files are more explicit line by line.
Use one format in a location: if both exist there, Spring Boot gives `.properties` precedence.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`application.properties` and `application.yml` are two ways to express Spring Boot configuration. They ultimately create property keys in the same Spring `Environment`, so choosing YAML does not unlock a different configuration system.

A properties file is flat: each line repeats the full key, such as `app.client.timeout=2s`. YAML represents the same key through indentation under `app` and `client`. That can make a large nested structure or a list easier to read, while a small properties file is often simpler because every value is visible on one line.

The main YAML risk is whitespace. Indentation changes structure, tabs are not valid indentation, and values that look like booleans or numbers may need careful quoting for the intended type. Properties files repeat prefixes but are straightforward to compare and override. Spring's binder can map either representation to the same typed `@ConfigurationProperties` object.

I choose the format the team can read and maintain consistently. I avoid keeping both `application.properties` and `application.yml` in the same location because Spring Boot gives the properties file precedence, which can hide an expected YAML value. The decision is about readability and team convention, not performance or capability.

sections.title: The same settings written in two shapes
sections.content:
Spring Boot supports `.properties`, `.yaml`, and `.yml` config-data files. After loading, both formats contribute named values to the `Environment`. Code that injects `app.client.timeout` does not need to know which file supplied it.

In a properties file, hierarchy is written into every key. This repetition is useful when searching for one exact property and makes a line easy to copy into an environment variable or command-line override. It becomes noisy when many entries share a long prefix.

YAML removes repeated prefixes by nesting child keys under their parent. It also represents lists naturally. The trade-off is that indentation carries meaning, so one misplaced space can move a value to a different path. A YAML document can contain multiple logical documents, but using that feature well requires understanding Spring's activation rules.

The binder normalizes the two examples below to the same keys. A component using `@ConfigurationProperties("app.client")` can receive `baseUrl`, `timeout`, and `regions` from either file. This is why a format migration should not require business-code changes when the effective keys remain the same.

Spring Boot recommends choosing one format for a location. If both a properties file and a YAML file are present in the same location, `.properties` wins. Mixing them may produce a valid application with a surprising effective value, which is harder to diagnose than a clear parse error.

sections.title: Properties and YAML at a glance
sections.content:
| Concern | `application.properties` | `application.yml` |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | Flat `key=value` lines | Indented mappings and sequences |
| Repeated prefixes | Yes | Usually grouped once |
| Lists | Indexed or comma-separated binding forms | Natural sequence syntax |
| Main editing risk | Long or mistyped keys | Wrong indentation or unintended scalar type |
| Spring result | Values in the `Environment` | The same `Environment` property keys |

sections.title: Equivalent client settings
sections.content:
```properties
app.client.base-url=https://api.example
app.client.timeout=2s
app.client.regions[0]=in-south
app.client.regions[1]=eu-west
```

```yaml
app:
  client:
    base-url: https://api.example
    timeout: 2s
    regions:
      - in-south
      - eu-west
```

Both files expose the keys under `app.client`; the binder can create the same Java configuration object from either one.

questions.question: How do you change the server port in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Configuring server.port in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Set `server.port` to the required port—for example `server.port=9090`. The value can come from an application file, the `SERVER_PORT` environment variable, a Java system property, or a command-line argument.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Set `server.port=9090` in application configuration to use port 9090.
The default HTTP port for a normal Spring Boot web application is 8080.
`SERVER_PORT=9090` and `--server.port=9090` are useful deployment-time forms.
Place `-Dserver.port=9090` before `-jar` when using a Java system property.
Use `server.port=0` in tests or local parallel runs when any free port is acceptable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The embedded web server reads the `server.port` property. I can set `server.port=9090` in `application.properties`, or write the equivalent YAML setting. If no port is configured, a normal Spring Boot web application uses port 8080.

For deployment, I usually override the packaged default instead of editing the JAR. Common forms are `SERVER_PORT=9090`, `java -Dserver.port=9090 -jar app.jar`, and `java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090`. When several sources provide the property, Spring Boot's normal precedence decides the effective value; the command-line form is higher than the system property and environment variable in the common runtime sources.

Setting `server.port=0` asks the operating system to choose an available port. That is useful for integration tests and for running several local instances without guessing unused ports. A Spring Boot web test can inject the selected value with `@LocalServerPort`.

Changing the listening port only changes where this process accepts connections. A reverse proxy, container port mapping, firewall, service discovery entry, or health check may also need the new port. I verify the effective startup log and send a request through the same path that real traffic will use.

beats.recallRule: Set server.port, choose the source by environment, and verify every network layer that points to the process.

sections.title: Changing the port from local development to deployment
sections.content:
`server.port` is a Spring Boot server setting, not a Tomcat-only switch. The web-server auto-configuration applies it to the embedded server selected by the application. The same property therefore works with the supported servlet and reactive server arrangements where the server factory exposes a port.

A file value is convenient as a local default. An environment variable or command-line argument is better when a platform assigns the port. Spring Boot's relaxed environment binding maps `SERVER_PORT` to `server.port`, so a deployment does not need to rewrite the packaged file.

The position of a Java system property matters to the Java launcher: `java -Dserver.port=9090 -jar app.jar` is correct. Text after the JAR name is passed to the application instead. Spring Boot's command-line property form is `java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090`.

Port zero has a special meaning. It does not make the server listen on a literal port 0; it asks the operating system to allocate a currently free port. Because that value is known only after startup, tests should read the assigned port from the running application rather than assume one.

A successful bind does not prove external reachability. In a container, `server.port` is the internal listening port while published host or service ports may differ. A complete check includes the startup log, an application health request, and the routing configuration in front of the process.

sections.title: Ways to supply the same port setting
sections.content:
| Source | Example | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Properties file | `server.port=9090` | Safe packaged or local default |
| Environment variable | `SERVER_PORT=9090` | Container or deployment configuration |
| Java system property | `-Dserver.port=9090` before `-jar` | JVM launch configuration |
| Command-line argument | `--server.port=9090` | One-run override |
| Random port | `server.port=0` | Integration tests or parallel local runs |

questions.question: What is the Spring Boot property hierarchy and what takes highest precedence?
questions.title: Spring Boot property source hierarchy
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot's property-source hierarchy is the ordered list used to choose an effective configuration value. Among common runtime sources, command-line arguments override Java system properties, which override operating-system environment variables, which override application config data; test-specific sources can rank even higher.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Spring Boot keeps property sources in an order; the higher-priority value wins for the same key.
For common runtime inputs: command line > Java system properties > OS environment variables > config data.
Within config data, profile-specific files override non-profile files at the same location.
External config files can override equivalent files packaged inside the JAR.
The complete order also includes test, servlet/JNDI, JSON, and other sources, so inspect the effective Environment when debugging.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot does not read configuration from one file only. It creates an ordered `Environment` from property files, profile files, environment variables, Java system properties, command-line arguments, test configuration, and several other sources. When the same key appears more than once, the higher-priority source supplies the effective value.

For the common runtime sources, I remember the order as command-line arguments above Java system properties, above operating-system environment variables, above application config data. So if the file has `server.port=8080`, `SERVER_PORT` is 9090, `-Dserver.port` is 6060, and the command line contains `--server.port=7070`, the application uses 7070.

Config data has its own ordering. A profile-specific file overrides the non-profile file at the same location, and an external file can override the corresponding file packaged in the JAR. This supports a useful pattern: package safe defaults, add environment-specific overlays, then reserve high-priority sources for deployment overrides.

Command line is not the absolute highest source in every situation. Spring Boot also defines test-specific property sources that can outrank it, and the full list includes `SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON`, servlet configuration, and JNDI where applicable. In a configuration bug, I check the effective value and its origin instead of guessing from one file.

beats.spokenText: Spring Boot does not read configuration from one file only. It creates an ordered `Environment` from property files, profile files, environment variables, Java system properties, command-line arguments, test configuration, and several other sources. When the same key appears more than once, the higher-priority source supplies the effective value.

For the common runtime sources, I remember the order as command-line arguments above Java system properties, above operating-system environment variables, above application config data. So if the file has `server.port=8080`, `SERVER_PORT` is 9090, `-Dserver.port` is 6060, and the command line contains `--server.port=7070`, the application uses 7070.

Config data has its own ordering. A profile-specific file overrides the non-profile file at the same location, and an external file can override the corresponding file packaged in the JAR. This supports a useful pattern: package safe defaults, add environment-specific overlays, then reserve high-priority sources for deployment overrides.

beats.stage: Runtime shorthand is not the full list
beats.spokenText: Command line is not the absolute highest source in every situation. Spring Boot also defines test-specific property sources that can outrank it, and the full list includes `SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON`, servlet configuration, and JNDI where applicable. In a configuration bug, I check the effective value and its origin instead of guessing from one file.
beats.recallRule: For normal deployment overrides, remember CLI > system property > environment > config data, then consult the full order for tests and special sources.

sections.title: Why the same key can have several values
sections.content:
Externalized configuration lets the same application artifact run in different places. A packaged file can define a safe default, an external file can adapt it to one environment, and a launch-time source can make a temporary override. Spring Boot orders these sources so the result is predictable.

The common deployment order is easy to demonstrate. Config data is below operating-system environment variables, environment variables are below Java system properties, and system properties are below command-line arguments. Only the value from the highest source for a key is returned, while unrelated lower-source keys remain available.

Config-data ordering is more detailed than simply 'the profile wins.' Non-profile files load before profile-specific files, and packaged files load before external files. Location groups and an explicit `spring.config.location` can affect the search, so production code should not assume every file on disk is automatically equal.

Spring Boot's complete property-source list also includes defaults set by the application, `@PropertySource`, `SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON`, servlet and JNDI sources, test annotations, and development tools. Some of these exist only in certain environments. That is why command line should be described as highest among the usual runtime deployment inputs, not as an unconditional top source.

A reliable investigation starts with the effective property rather than the expected file. Actuator's environment endpoint can show origins when exposed safely, and startup diagnostics or a focused test can confirm the winner. Sensitive values must be sanitized; debugging precedence is not a reason to print credentials.

sections.title: Common runtime sources from higher to lower priority
sections.content:
| Priority | Source | Example for `server.port` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — highest in this common subset | Command-line argument | `--server.port=7070` |
| 2 | Java system property | `-Dserver.port=6060` |
| 3 | OS environment variable | `SERVER_PORT=9090` |
| 4 | Application config data | `server.port=8080` |
| Below this subset | Application defaults | A default supplied by code |

sections.title: Four sources define one key
sections.content:
```properties
# application.properties
server.port=8080
```

```bash
SERVER_PORT=9090 java -Dserver.port=6060 -jar app.jar --server.port=7070
```

The effective value is `7070` because the command-line property outranks the system property, environment variable, and config file in this set.

questions.question: What is spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto and what are its values?
questions.title: spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto configuration
questions.direct_answer: `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` is the Spring Boot setting that tells Hibernate what schema action to take when the persistence unit starts. The five common values are `none`, `validate`, `update`, `create`, and `create-drop`; production systems usually use a migration tool and choose `validate` or `none`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `none` performs no automatic schema action.
`validate` checks that the existing schema matches the entity mapping and fails on a mismatch.
`update` tries to adjust an existing schema, but it is not a versioned, reviewable migration plan.
`create` rebuilds the schema at startup; `create-drop` also drops it when the persistence unit closes.
For production, prefer Flyway or Liquibase migrations and normally pair them with `validate` or `none`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` controls Hibernate's automatic schema action at startup. It compares or builds the database structure from JPA entity mappings, depending on the selected value. It is a schema-management setting; it does not migrate the application data with business-aware steps.

The common values are `none`, `validate`, `update`, `create`, and `create-drop`. `none` does nothing. `validate` checks the existing tables, columns, and mapping expectations and stops startup on a mismatch. `update` asks Hibernate to adjust the schema. `create` drops and recreates the schema when the persistence unit starts, while `create-drop` also drops it when the persistence unit shuts down.

For a disposable local database or an isolated test, `create-drop` can be convenient because every run starts clean. I avoid `create` and `create-drop` for persistent data. I also avoid treating `update` as a production migration tool: it has no reviewed migration history or rollback plan, and changes such as a column rename may not be interpreted as the intended safe data move.

In production I use Flyway or Liquibase for ordered schema changes and usually set Hibernate to `validate` so mapping mistakes fail at startup, or `none` when validation is handled elsewhere. Spring Boot's default is `create-drop` only for an embedded database when no schema manager is detected; otherwise it is `none`, so I prefer to configure the intended policy explicitly.

beats.spokenText: `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` controls Hibernate's automatic schema action at startup. It is a schema-management setting; it does not migrate the application data with business-aware steps.

beats.recallRule: Generate disposable schemas for tests; migrate persistent schemas with versioned scripts and let Hibernate validate.

sections.title: How ddl-auto changes the database schema
sections.content:
Hibernate knows the entity model and can derive tables, columns, constraints, and sequences from that mapping. The `ddl-auto` setting selects an action for the database schema when the persistence unit starts. Spring Boot passes this choice to Hibernate through its schema-management integration.

`validate` is read-only with respect to schema creation: it checks that the database is compatible with the mappings and reports a mismatch. `update` attempts changes in place. Because the generated operation depends on the Hibernate version and database dialect, it is not a substitute for an explicit migration that a team can review, test, order, and roll back.

`create` rebuilds the schema at startup, so existing objects and data are at risk. `create-drop` performs the startup rebuild and schedules another drop when the persistence unit closes. Those behaviors are valuable for short-lived tests but unsafe for any database whose data must survive an application restart.

The five values in the table are the common Spring Boot interview set. The Hibernate version managed by Spring Boot 3.3.1 also recognizes lower-level actions such as `create-only` and `drop`. They are specialized choices, and accepted names can depend on the managed Hibernate version; the application should not guess a value from a different release.

Spring Boot chooses a default based on database and schema-manager detection: an embedded database without Flyway or Liquibase normally gets `create-drop`; other cases normally get `none`. An explicit production setting is easier to review. A typical production arrangement lets Flyway or Liquibase apply versioned changes before JPA starts and uses `validate` to catch mapping drift.

A column rename shows why ownership matters. A migration can rename the column and transform existing data in a known order. Automatic update only sees a difference between mappings and schema; it does not know the business intent, compatibility window, or rollback plan. Persistent data deserves a versioned migration.

sections.title: The five common ddl-auto values
sections.content:
| Value | What Hibernate does | Suitable use |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | No automatic schema action | Production when another tool owns schema checks and changes |
| `validate` | Checks mappings against the existing schema | Production after versioned migrations |
| `update` | Attempts to adjust the schema in place | Limited local experiments; not controlled production migration |
| `create` | Drops and recreates the schema at startup | Disposable development data only |
| `create-drop` | Creates at startup and drops again at shutdown | Isolated tests or disposable demos |

sections.title: Use different schema policies for disposable and persistent data
sections.content:
```properties
# application-dev.properties — disposable local database
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
```

```properties
# application-prod.properties — migrations own schema changes
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.flyway.enabled=true
```

The production profile lets migration scripts make ordered changes and asks Hibernate only to confirm that the resulting schema matches the entity mappings.
